title: mini-sdks-onramp-experiential-quickpaths-draft
content:
Purpose
----
A compact, experiment-first outline for a family of mini SDKs and 10-minute onramps aimed at product engineers and platform teams. Focus: remove friction for first successful inference call, then give progressive steps for reliability, cost control, and observability. This doc is intentionally terse — sprint notes + lab checklist style — not a full PRD.

TL;DR (for PM/Eng lead)
----
- Deliver 3 opinionated mini SDK packages (Python/Node/Go) that get a dev from zero to a streaming generation in <10 minutes with example app and local replayable tests.
- Prioritize ergonomic defaults: safe timeouts, built-in retry/backoff, streaming examples, and token cost estimation hooks.
- Provide a one-page quickstart (copy/paste) + a troubleshooting checklist for the first 5 failure modes we see in labs.

Audience
----
- Product engineers adding an LLM feature to a product (fast validation).
- Platform engineers who want reproducible examples to embed in infra docs.
- Solutions engineers who need a short demo path for customers.

Success metrics (experiment phase)
----
- Time-to-first-successful-call median <= 10 minutes in user tests (target 8m).
- >60% of test users complete the mini-lab without mentor help.
- Reduction in "setup" support tickets referencing SDK onboarding by 30% in first quarter after release.
- Telemetry: emit 'onboarding_completed' event when quickstart run; capture failures.

Deliverables (MVP scope)
----
1) mini-sdk-python (pip install redwood-mini-sdk)
   - single-file example: minimal_client.py
   - streaming example: stream_chat.py (websocket fallback demo)
   - local mock server for offline dev (docker compose)
   - tests: simple replay harness + golden prompt set
2) mini-sdk-node (npm)
   - identical surface; copy/paste examples for express and next.js
3) mini-sdk-go (module)
   - CLI-first example; highlight sync/async patterns
4) one-page quickstart markdown + four GIFs (install, auth, first call, streaming)
5) troubleshooting checklist (top 5 failure modes + quick fixes)
6) telemetry spec and minimal instrumentation (events + error tags)

Step-by-step quick path (developer flow)
----
1) Install package (1 command)
2) Set environment var REDWOOD_API_KEY or run 'redwood login'
3) Run: python minimal_client.py — should print response and cost estimate
4) Optional: run stream_chat.py and poke the websocket endpoint in 2 tabs
5) Run local mock server: docker compose up && point SDK at http://localhost:8080

Example minimal_client.py (in doc form, tiny)
----
# pseudo code, for copy/paste
from redwood_mini import RedwoodClient
client = RedwoodClient(api_key=os.getenv('REDWOOD_API_KEY'))
res = client.generate("Write a haiku about latency")
print(res.text)
print("est tokens:", res.estimate.tokens)

Notes: keep the example under 30 lines, avoid complex config. Use a friendly default model (redwood/fast-small) and small max_tokens=64 to limit cost.

Observability & telemetry (MVP)
----
- Emit onboarding_started, onboarding_step_completed (step id), onboarding_failed (error_code), onboarding_completed.
- Attach metadata: sdk_lang, sdk_version, flow_variant (quickstart|labs|cli), environment (local|cloud).
- Log token estimate and actual token count when available.
- Implementation: SDK emits events to internal telemetry endpoint; the quickstart will include a flag to opt-in during dev.

Failure modes & quick fixes (labs-derived)
----
1) 401 due to API key scoping -> quick fix: set REDWOOD_API_KEY or run 'redwood login', show how to check key scopes in console
2) Connection timeout (on low-bandwidth) -> quick fix: increase timeout, enable reconnect/backoff sample
3) Streaming didn't start (CORS/mismatch) -> quick fix: point to websocket example and common browser header problem
4) Local mock mismatch -> quick fix: include a versioned mock image and sample curl to verify
5) Unexpected high token cost -> quick fix: reduce max_tokens, add 'estimate_tokens' helper, show cost calculation snippet

Developer labs and tests (playful, quick feedback)
----
- 3 guided labs (15–30 min each):
  Lab A: Hello world generation + assert expected string match (golden prompt)
  Lab B: Streaming UI with reconnection simulation (network flaps)
  Lab C: Cost-aware batching demo (send 50 small prompts as batch and compare cost/latency)
- Each lab includes a grading script that returns PASS/FAIL, so new hires / customers can self-validate.

Rollout & docs plan (phases)
----
Phase 0 (internal alpha) — 2 weeks
- Package python proof-of-concept, run on internal infra, iterate with SRE on timeouts and retry defaults.
Phase 1 (wider eng preview) — 3 weeks
- Publish node/go, add GIFs, record 5min screencast, gather 20 engineers for usability test.
Phase 2 (public beta) — 4 weeks
- Publish to package registries, add telemetry, surface quickstart in Console "Try SDK" button.
Phase 3 (GA) — dependent on telemetry and support ticket reduction target.

Open questions / tradeoffs (notes to self)
----
- How opinionated should defaults be? e.g., auto-batching on by default could surprise devs. Maybe opt-in with a one-liner sample.
- Should the mini-sdk include tokenizers for cost estimation offline, or rely on server-side estimates? Offline gives faster feedback but increases package size.
- Level of mocking fidelity: full protocol or just obvious happy-path stubs? Full fidelity increases maintenance burden.
- Legal: any sample prompts with PII? Avoid, but include a secured prompts note. 

Links / references (for follow-up)
----
- GH starter PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/sdk-starter/pull/412
- UX examples: confluence:Onboarding-Roadmap-2026
- Telemetry ticket: JIRA:DX-285

Next steps (short term)
----
- [ ] Spin up internal alpha repo and publish python mini package to internal pip
- [ ] Create 3 short GIFs for copy/paste quickstart
- [ ] Draft instrumentation + event names and share with analytics
- [ ] Schedule 30m lab run with 10 dev volunteers (target next sprint)

Random notes (brain dump)
----
- Consider embedding a tiny browser-based playground that runs against the local mock for sales demos.
- Keep examples under 30s runtime to ensure clickable demos in docs.
- Avoid using 'auto' model names in examples; reference the catalog tag (e.g., redwood/fast-small@v1) so examples are stable.

(End of draft — concise, experimental, needs review by DX, SRE, and legal before public docs.)
